How are speed, frequency and period related?



Two boats bob up and down once every two seconds. How fast is the wave?

Learning Objectives

What you'll be able to do

  • Define and use the terms speed, frequency, wavelength, period and amplitude.
  • Use graphs of waves, including displacement against time.
  • Recall and apply speed of wave = frequency x wavelength.
  • Use that relationship in new situations and to solve related problems.

Core concept
Two graphs

Two graphs that look the same

The transverse rope wave can also be represented using a displacement-time graph.

Learn
  • A displacement-time graph tracks the displacement of one particle over a period of time.Pick one point on the rope and watch only that point. Plot how high it is, second by second. That is a displacement-time graph.
    • displacement-time graph

    This graph shows how one particular particle moves over time.

    • Horizontal axis: time
    • Vertical axis: displacement from the rest position
    • It answers: “How does this one particle move as time passes?”
    • The time from one crest to the next crest is the period, T.

    Imagine choosing one coloured dot on the skipping rope and recording its up-and-down movement.

  • A displacement-distance graph shows the whole wave at one instant, which is what all of you have mostly been learning about.This one is a snapshot. Freeze the rope and measure the height everywhere along it.
    • Displacement-distance graph

    This graph shows the positions of many different particles at one particular moment.

    • Horizontal axis: distance along the wave
    • Vertical axis: displacement from the rest position
    • It answers: “What does the whole wave look like right now?”
    • The distance from one crest to the next crest is the wavelength, λ.

    Imagine taking one photograph of a long skipping rope. You can see where every part of the rope is at that instant.

Key Facts
  • Horizontal axis in metres: one complete wave is the wavelength.
  • Horizontal axis in seconds: one complete wave is the period.
  • Amplitude can be read off either graph, from the vertical axis.
Test

A graph of a wave has time on its horizontal axis. One complete wave spans 0.5 s. What does 0.5 s represent?

Core concept
The wave equation

Period, frequency and wave speed

Let's explore the three different characteristics :]

Learn
  • The period (T) is the time taken to produce one complete wave. Its SI unit is the second (s).How long one whole wave takes. Watch one cork: the time from one crest to the next is the period.
  • The frequency (f) is the number of complete waves produced in one second. Its SI unit is the hertz (Hz).How many whole waves go past every second. Two waves a second is 2 Hz.
  • The wave speed (v) is the distance travelled by a wave per second. Its SI unit is m/s.
  • Frequency and period are linked. f = 1 / T, and T = 1 / f.
Key Facts
  • v = f λ. Wave speed equals frequency times wavelength.
  • f = 1 / T. A period of 2 s means a frequency of 0.5 Hz.
  • Check the unit before you check the arithmetic: Hz, s, m and m/s.
Test

A boat on a wave completes one full oscillation every 4.0 s. What is the frequency of the wave?

✦Beyond the syllabusWhere v = f lambda actually comes from

Not examinable. Worth knowing anyway.

NOT EXAMINABLE · PURELY DELICIOUS

Why does this work at all? Because a crest leaving the source every T seconds has already travelled one wavelength by the time the next one leaves. That is the whole derivation, and it is one sentence long. Physicists call a quantity that refuses to move under changing conditions an invariant, and hunting for them is most of what theoretical physics is.

✦Beyond the syllabusYour phone does this two billion times a second

Not examinable. Worth knowing anyway.

NOT EXAMINABLE · PURELY DELICIOUS

Your phone is doing this 2,400,000,000 times a second. Wi-fi runs at about 2.4 GHz, so f = 2.4 x 109 Hz. Put that into v = f λ with the speed of light and the wavelength comes out at about 12.5 cm, roughly the width of your hand. That is why a wi-fi antenna is the size it is, and why one spot in a flat kills the signal.

Practice: Example 7, reading a graph

Read a wavelength off the graph, then use it twice.

Example 70 / 6
1Two steps ask before they tell.

The graph shows a displacement-distance graph of a wave. The speed of the wave is 200 m/s. Find the wavelength, the frequency and the period.

v = 200 m/sλ = ? mf = ? HzT = ? s
  1. The wavelength in metres, the frequency in hertz, and the period in seconds.
  2. m
    One complete wave runs from the crest at 0 m to the next crest at 4 m.λ = 4.0 m
  3. v = f λ
  4. Hz
    f = v / λ = 200 / 4.0f = 50 Hz
  5. T = 1 / f = 1 / 50T = 0.020 sThe period is one divided by the frequency, always.
  6. Fifty waves a second, each 4 m long, is 200 m every second. That is the speed we were given, so the answer checks out.

Practice: Example 8, the two boats

Four numbers, and two of them belong to something else.

Example 80 / 6
1Three steps ask before they tell.

Two boats A and B are 50 m apart and a wave is travelling towards them. The wave takes 5.0 s to travel from boat A to boat B. The boats make one complete oscillation in 2.0 s. The boat rises 1.5 m from its lowest position to its highest position. Determine the amplitude, the frequency and the velocity.

distance A to B = 50 mtime = 5.0 sone oscillation = 2.0 srise = 1.5 m
  1. 50 m and 5.0 s belong to the wave travelling. 2.0 s and 1.5 m belong to a boat bobbing. Mixing the two is the usual mistake here.
  2. m
    Trough to crest is twice the amplitude, because amplitude is measured from the rest position.a = 1.5 / 2a = 0.75 m
  3. f = 1 / T
  4. f = 1 / 2.0f = 0.50 HzOne complete oscillation every 2.0 s is half a wave each second.
  5. m/s
    v = distance / time = 50 / 5.0v = 10 m/s
  6. 10 m/s at 0.50 Hz gives a wavelength of 20 m, so 50 m holds two and a half waves. That fits boats one on a crest and one in a trough.

Practice: Example 9, water and light

The same equation twice, in wildly different units.

Example 90 / 6
1Three steps ask before they tell.

(b) A water wave has a frequency of 2.0 Hz and a wavelength of 0.30 m. How fast is it moving? (c) Purple light has a speed of 3.0 × 108 m/s and a frequency of 5.0 × 1014 Hz. What is its wavelength?

(b) f = 2.0 Hzλ = 0.30 m(c) v = 3.0 × 108 m/sf = 5.0 × 1014 Hz
  1. v = f λ
  2. m/s
    v = 2.0 × 0.30v = 0.60 m/s
  3. λ = v / fStandard form numbers are much easier to handle once the algebra is done.
  4. λ = (3.0 × 108) / (5.0 × 1014)λ = 6.0 × 10-7 mDivide the front numbers, then subtract the powers: 8 − 14 = −6, and 3.0 / 5.0 = 0.6, so 0.6 × 10-6.
  5. nm
    1 nm = 10-9 m, so 6.0 × 10-7 m = 600 nm600 nm
  6. Visible light runs from about 400 nm to 700 nm, so 600 nm sits inside the visible range. A purple answer near 400 nm would be better still, which is worth a question in class.

Practice: answer, then say why

Assess

Two tiers

A right answer for the wrong reason is still a problem. This item finds it.

Answer, then say whyTwo tiers
1Pick an answer, pick the reason, then say how sure you are.

A ripple tank dipper is set to a higher frequency. The water depth is not touched. What happens to the wave speed?

Tier 1 — what happens
Tier 2 — why it happens
Go back to the rope lab. Set the frequency to its lowest, read the speed, then set it to its highest and read the speed again. The number does not move. Now change the stiffness slider instead and watch it move immediately. The medium owns the speed.
Check the direction. Shallower or heavier means slower. Nothing in this question changed the water at all, so the speed had nothing to respond to.
They are related. v = f λ ties all three together. The question is which of the three is held fixed: in one medium it is v.
Only one can rise. With v pinned, f and λ trade off. Double one and the other halves. They cannot both go up.
